Eggs of Hutton's shearwater (Puffinus huttoni) are incubated for an average of 50.3 days [ab = 50.3 days] when maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a developmental duration that aligns closely with incubation periods reported for other small procellariiform seabirds. Upon hatching, the chicks emerge with a wet weight at birth of approximately 60 grams [Wwb = approximately 60 grams], a modest starting mass that reflects the relatively limited yolk reserves typical of species that experience a prolonged nestling phase. This initial size is substantially smaller than the peak mass that nestlings must achieve during development, underscoring the considerable growth challenge faced during the subsequent weeks in the high-altitude burrows of the Kaikoura Ranges. Field observations indicate that the incubation temperature, maintained by the attending parents through constant brood patch contact, is critical for successful embryonic development. Deviations from this optimal thermal regime are known to prolong the incubation period or reduce hatching success, as documented in comparative studies of related Procellariidae species. The relatively long incubation period for a bird of this body mass is consistent with the slow life-history pace typical of pelagic seabirds.

Nestlings undergo a period of rapid mass gain, ultimately achieving an ultimate wet weight of 730 grams [Wwi = 730 grams] prior to fledging, a value that far exceeds the mean adult mass of approximately 358.8 grams for females and 373.7 grams for males. This substantial pre-fledging mass, fueled by regular provisioning of lipid-rich stomach oil and partially digested prey by both parents, serves as a critical energy reserve during the demanding transition to an independent existence at sea. The fledging event itself, marking the time since birth at fledging, occurs at 86 days after hatching [tx = 86 days after hatching] under the typical thermal conditions of the active chick-rearing period, which average 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C] within the well-insulated nest burrow. Reaching this developmental milestone requires the successful completion of feather growth and the attainment of sufficient flight muscle mass. This relatively extended nestling period is characteristic of the genus and is thought to be an adaptation to the unpredictable food supply typical of the neritic and oceanic waters the adults forage in.

Sexual maturation in Puffinus huttoni is a prolonged process, with the time since birth at puberty estimated at 258 days after hatching [tp = 258 days after hatching] when ambient conditions approximate 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C] during the active growth phases. However, this physiological milestone does not immediately translate into reproductive activity; the age at which individuals produce their first brood is considerably deferred. The time since birth at first brood is approximately 1,825 days [tR = approximately 1,825 days], a value that reflects the extended period required for young birds to acquire the necessary foraging skills and body condition to successfully rear offspring. at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]This multi-year delay to first breeding, during which subadults may return to natal colonies and engage in courtship behaviors without breeding, is a common life-history trait among long-lived seabirds and is thought to reduce the risks associated with early reproductive attempts. Breeding is typically initiated only after individuals have achieved a stable body mass and established a durable pair bond.

The maximum reproductive rate of this species is limited, with pairs typically raising a single egg per breeding attempt [N_R_i = single egg per breeding attempt] and producing a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually] during the spring and summer months when food resources are most abundant. This low fecundity, characteristic of the Procellariiformes, reflects an evolutionary trade-off favoring high parental investment in a single, robust offspring over the production of multiple, smaller young. The reproductive effort is further constrained by the energetic demands of long-distance foraging trips, which can span several days, during which one parent must remain at the burrow to incubate or guard the chick. Monogamous pair bonds, often maintained across multiple breeding seasons, contribute to the stability of reproductive output. The success of each nesting attempt is heavily dependent on the body condition of the adults at the start of the season, which in turn is influenced by the availability of prey such as krill and small fish.

Longevity data for Puffinus huttoni remain somewhat limited, but based on records from the closely related Manx shearwater (Puffinus puffinus), the estimated maximum lifespan is approximately 50.9 years [am = approximately 50.9 years] when individuals are free from unusual environmental stressors and maintain core body temperatures near 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This exceptional lifespan, among the longest recorded for any bird of its body size, is a cornerstone of the species' slow, K-selected life-history strategy. A long reproductive window, potentially spanning several decades, allows individuals to compensate for low annual fecundity by accumulating breeding attempts over a lifetime. The species faces significant natural mortality from introduced predators at their limited breeding colonies, which represent the entirety of the global population. Conservation efforts focused on predator control and habitat restoration are therefore critical for allowing individuals to realize their full physiological lifespan. The persistence of such long-lived pelagic foragers depends on the continued health of the marine ecosystems that sustain them during the non-breeding season.
